claims.text: The high-temperature structural stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by formation of a stable oxide shell.
The high-temperature chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by formation of a stable oxide shell.
A stable oxide shell prevents noble-metal diffusion.
A stable oxide shell prevents noble-metal aggregation.
Suppressing noble-metal diffusion and aggregation maintains nanoparticle structure.
Suppressing noble-metal diffusion and aggregation maintains nanoparticle composition.
Annealing at 973 K for 24 hours in an inert atmosphere will produce or stabilize the proposed oxide shell.
Annealed nanoparticles will have improved structural stability relative to as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles will have improved chemical stability relative to as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Annealing will cause minimal change in nanoparticle size.
Annealing will cause minimal change in nanoparticle shape.
Annealing will cause minimal change in nanoparticle composition.
The proposed hypothesis applies when noble-metal content is below 10 at.%.
The proposed hypothesis applies over 473–1923 K.
TEM, XPS, and EDS measurements can be used to compare morphology, surface chemistry, composition, and crystal structure between annealed and as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Significant noble-metal diffusion and aggregation after annealing would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies annealing in an inert atmosphere while assuming formation of an oxide shell, but no oxygen source, pre-existing oxide, or controlled oxygen exposure is specified.
The stated service conditions are 773–1173 K, whereas the claimed boundary is 473–1923 K; the hypothesis therefore claims applicability far outside the specified intervention and test range.
